title: The argument needs no present infallibility
source_text: XXXIV. Sed ut subsistat argumentum istud, & vim suam habeat, non necesse est ut praesentis Ecclesiae Pastores authoritatem habeant divinam & infallibilem, Scriptura ipsa quoad nos notiorem & superiorem. Nec argumentum istud simpliciter nititur eorum authoritate: sed vis argumenti in eo consistit, quod, si libri illi Apocryphi vere divini essent, & a Prophetis & Apostolis eo fine conscripti, ut perpetua essent in Ecclesia fidei regula, proculdubio a Prophetis & Apostolis ipsis pro talibus traditi & commendati fidelibus essent, ut alii libri Canonici, & cum reliquo Scripturae Canone consignati. At si hoc factum esset, Apostolici viri & Ecclesia proxime succedens Apostolis, quae tanta reverentia reliquos eorum libros suscepit, absque omni dubio istos quoque suscepisset, &, si non ab omnibus, saltem a maxima, aut notabili parte fidelium admissi fuissent. Itaque quod eorum ne meminerint quidem prisci Ecclesiae Doctores, signum est manifestum Apostolos, quum Canonem Scripturae consignarunt, ejusmodi libros non admisisse, sed rejecisse & repudiasse. Nec ullo modo verisimile est Deum singulari sua providentia Prophetam aut Apostolum ad scribendum impulisse, eo fine ut liber illius esset fidei regula in Ecclesia Dei, & ad eruditionem & consolationem fidelium inserviret, & tamen passum fuisse ut liber ille ab Ecclesia sua nec reciperetur nec agnosceretur.
pass_a_gloss: But for that argument to stand and have its force, it is not necessary that the Pastors of the present Church have a divine and infallible authority, better known and superior to us than Scripture itself. Nor does that argument simply rest on their authority: but the force of the argument consists in this, that if those Apocryphal books were truly divine, and written by the Prophets and Apostles for this end, that they should be a perpetual rule of faith in the Church, without doubt they would have been handed down and recommended to the faithful as such by the Prophets and Apostles themselves, like the other Canonical books, and sealed with the rest of the Canon of Scripture. But if this had been done, the Apostolic men and the Church next succeeding the Apostles, which received their other books with such reverence, would without any doubt have received these also, and, if not by all, at least by the greatest or a notable part of the faithful they would have been admitted. Therefore that the ancient Doctors of the Church do not even remember them is a manifest sign that the Apostles, when they sealed the Canon of Scripture, did not admit books of that kind, but rejected and repudiated them. Nor is it in any way likely that God by His singular providence impelled a Prophet or Apostle to write, to the end that his book should be a rule of faith in the Church of God and should serve for the instruction and consolation of the faithful, and yet suffered that that book should neither be received nor acknowledged by His Church.
pass_b_english: For that argument to stand, the pastors of the present Church need not have a divine, infallible authority better known to us and superior to Scripture itself.

The argument does not simply rest on their authority. Its force is this: if those apocryphal books were truly divine, and written by the prophets and apostles to be a perpetual rule of faith in the Church, the prophets and apostles themselves would without doubt have handed them down and recommended them as such — like the other canonical books, and sealed with the rest of Scripture's Canon.

Had that happened, the apostolic men and the Church next after the apostles, which received their other books with such reverence, would without doubt have received these too — if not among all the faithful, at least among the greatest or a notable part.
That the ancient Church doctors do not even mention them is a clear sign that the apostles, when they sealed Scripture's Canon, did not admit such books, but rejected and cast them out.

It is in no way likely that God by His singular providence moved a prophet or apostle to write so that his book would be a rule of faith and serve the faithful's instruction and comfort — and yet allowed His Church neither to receive nor to acknowledge that book.
